GEOH2-01.note: No figure; none needed, the equation is the whole stimulus. Complete the square, set y=0, double. Two routine steps, so medium against the real hard route. PARTIAL OPTION-SET TELL: the set {15, 34, 30, 12} hands you 34 (the diameter, so r=17) and 15 (the half-chord) alongside 30; seeing that one option is exactly double another, and a third is double the radius, lets a blind solver reconstruct the 8-15-17 triple and pick 30 without touching the equation. Not the a+b*pi form, but the same class of leak: the givens are recoverable from the options. Distractors are all named paths (half-chord, diameter, RHS misread).

GEOH2-02.note: No figure; a sketch helps but 'B lies on the same straight line between A and the base' pins the configuration unambiguously in words. Graded medium, not hard: this is a stock two-station-elevation template, every quantity is cued, and once h/tan(32) - h/tan(47) = 50 is written the calculator finishes it. The one real trap, 74.9 (the tower height, the quantity you solve for first), is exactly the 'one step short' distractor that recurs across this batch. 111.7 (tangents subtracted instead of reciprocals) and 31.2 are both endpoints of named errors.

GEOH2-03.note: No figure; the parenthetical '(two radii plus the arc)' removes the one thing a figure would have carried, and is the right call. Genuinely hard: two conditions in two unknowns collapse to a quadratic, BOTH roots are geometrically legal, and the angle-greater-than-2-radians clause is a third step that has to be recognised as a root selector rather than decoration. 12.0 (the rejected root) is the strongest distractor in the batch. No reconstruction from the option set: 2.4 and 24.0 are downstream of the answer, not inputs.

GEOH2-04.note: No figure and none needed. Hard on the real scale: the student must infer 'equal volumes' means the small cone is HALF the whole (not half the height), apply a cube-root scale factor, and then subtract from 24 because the question measures from the BASE while the similarity works from the apex. Three independent places to fall out, and each has an option waiting (19.0 apex height, 12.0 linear halving, 7.0 square instead of cube). Rounding is safe: 4.951, not a boundary. No option-set leak.

GEOH2-05.note: No figure; the right angle at C and the altitude from C to AB are stated, so the configuration is unambiguous without one, though this is an item where a figure would genuinely have earned its place. Medium, not hard, and the reason matters: the only real step is knowing the altitude-to-hypotenuse geometric-mean relation (pq = h^2), after which p+q=26, pq=144 is a one-line quadratic. That relation is off the Digital SAT content spec, so the item's apparent difficulty is knowledge-gated rather than reasoning-gated. Also check the givens are feasible: h=12 < 13, so the triangle exists. 18.0/14.4/13.0 are all real wrong endpoints.

GEOH2-06.note: No figure; 'two sides of length 13' fixes the legs and the text is unambiguous. Hard: the substitution u=(b/2)^2 turns the area condition into a quadratic with two legal triangles (b=10 and b=24), the stem's 'there is more than one such triangle' is a hint that still has to be acted on, and then the perimeter must be assembled rather than read off. 24.0 (the third side) and 36.0 (the other perimeter) are both exactly what a student stops at. Minor option-set observation, not disqualifying: 36 = 26+10 and 50 = 26+24, so both perimeters carry the visible 26 from the stem; that reveals the shape of the answer but not which root wins, which is the actual work.

GEOH2-07.note: No figure needed. 'k is positive' cleanly kills the -10 branch, so exclusive. Medium: solvable either by the point-line distance formula or by substitution and discriminant = 0, and the latter is standard SAT technique. Distractors are the weakest set in the batch: 4.5 (the radius) is a real stopping point, but 22.4 (multiply by 5 instead of sqrt 5) and 6.3 (divide by sqrt 2 because there are two coefficients) are both manufactured denominators rather than errors I can name a student making. Marked plausible on the strength of 4.5 alone.

GEOH2-08.note: No figure; two triangles named by vertex with the right angles stated, unambiguous. Medium: sin(A)=cos(D) implies A+D=90 is a College Board staple, and the only extension is one subtraction to reach angle F. Worth flagging that the key 33 coincidentally equals angle A, so a student who stops early at A still lands on the key by accident; that inflates the measured p-value without the item being easier. Distractors 57 (angle D), 14 (y), 45 (reading sin=cos as A=D) are all named paths.

GEOH2-09.note: No figure, none needed. Two chained standard facts (interior/exterior supplementary, then n(n-3)/2). Medium; nothing here discriminates at the top of the hard route. 18 (sides), 20 (exterior angle) and 153 (nC2, counting sides as diagonals) are three distinct real errors, the last of them the good one.

GEOH2-10.note: No figure. Exclusive: 'percent of the water that was ORIGINALLY IN THE TANK' names the denominator explicitly, which is the whole game here. Graded medium and I want to be explicit that this is the fiddly-not-hard case the brief warns about: unit conversion, a rate times a time, and a percent, all mechanically easy, with the difficulty sitting entirely in bookkeeping and a calculator. The distractor set is excellent precisely because it is a denominator sweep (40.2 remaining/capacity, 39.8 drained/capacity, 60.2 the mixed pair), but a long arithmetic chain is not hard-route difficulty.

GEOH2-11.note: No figure; 'terminal ray in the second quadrant' does the work a diagram would. Medium: 3-4-5 reference triangle plus two sign decisions. 2.15 (all signs positive), 0.55 (cosine negative but tangent left positive) and -1.53 (tangent inverted) are three cleanly separated error paths, and 0.55 in particular catches the half-correct student. Note this is the only negative key in the batch, and the only item whose option set is not all-positive; a solver who has noticed that the batch otherwise answers with plausible positive magnitudes gets nothing from it, but it is worth knowing the sign is not a tell here since two options are negative.

GEOH2-12.note: No figure; 'chords AB and CD intersect at P inside the circle', with CP<PD stated, is fully determined in text, and CP<PD is what makes it exclusive. Medium: the intersecting-chords product is off the SAT spec but universally drilled in prep, and once written the quadratic x^2-19x+60 is trivial. Same shape as GEOH2-05 (two numbers, sum and product, pick the smaller root) - see the cross-item note. 15.0 is the sibling root, 9.5 the bisection assumption, 6.0 the CP=AP confusion.

GEOH2-13.note: No figure; the four vertices are given as coordinates, which is strictly better than a figure here. Hard, and the best hard item in the batch: the equal-area segment is the root-mean-square of the bases, a result almost nobody has memorised, so it has to be derived from a linear-width model and a quadratic in y. 7.5 (the midsegment) is a near-lethal distractor because midsegment is the fact students DO have, and 7.1 (geometric mean) catches the student who half-remembers that a mean of the bases is involved. Nothing in the option set reconstructs the bases 10 and 5.

GEOH2-14.note: No figure. Medium: the square/cube scaling of similar solids is squarely on-spec and this is the textbook execution of it. 288 (applying the area ratio 9/4 to volume) and 192 (applying the linear ratio 3/2 uncubed) are both genuine, but 384 - 'multiply by 3 because 3 is the numerator of 3/2' - is a number from nowhere; no student who has got as far as extracting 3/2 then discards the 2. One manufactured distractor in four drops this to plausible.

GEOH2-15.note: No figure; 'circle inscribed in a right triangle, legs 9 and 12' is unambiguous. Medium: one insight (r=3, via (a+b-c)/2 or Area/s), then subtract. OPTION-SET TELL, and this is the recorded decidable tell in decimal clothing: the set is {54.0, 35.2, 25.7, 28.3} and 54.0 - 28.3 = 25.7 exactly. 54 is the triangle, 28.3 is 9pi. A blind solver who notices one option is the difference of two others picks the key without ever finding the inradius - which is the ONLY real step in the item. The composite is decimalised rather than written a - b*pi, so the existing pi-form check will not catch it. Recommend replacing 54.0 or 28.3 (e.g. with an r=2.5 or r=4 variant) so the difference relation no longer closes. Distractor paths themselves are all named and strong.

GEOH2-16.note: No figure needed. Verified by distance: (-3.5,0) is sqrt(31.25) from both A and B. Medium: perpendicular bisector, or set the two squared distances equal, which is the faster and fully on-spec route. -2.0 (the midpoint's x) and -1.5 (the displacement reported without adding the midpoint back) are both real slips; -0.5 (sign-flipped perpendicular slope) is weaker but legitimate. All four options negative, so sign gives nothing away.

GEOH2-17.note: No figure. Medium: two memorised volume formulas, one division, one floor. The floor step ('complete cylinders') is the only twist and is explicitly cued by the word 'complete', so 14 is a trap the stem already warns against. 41 (dropping the 1/3) and 8 (dividing surface area by volume, dimensionally nonsense but a real panic move) round out a strong set. The pi cancels exactly, so no option-set arithmetic leaks the radius.

GEOH2-18.note: No figure; 'same-side interior angle paired with it' names the relationship outright, which is what makes it exclusive AND what makes it easy - a real SAT item would show the transversal and make you identify the pair yourself. One linear equation, then pick the acute of 98/82. This is an early-module item, not a hard-route one, and it is the clearest case in the batch of a commissioned-hard slot coming back below band. Distractors are fine (98 obtuse, 22 the x-value, 58 from treating the pair as alternate interior).

GEOH2-19.note: No figure; a chord in a circle needs none, though the perpendicular-from-centre construction is mental work. 'Smaller of the two regions' makes it exclusive. Hard: circular-segment area = sector minus triangle, requiring arcsin for the central angle and then a sector-area-in-radians formula; this is at or past the edge of the Digital SAT domain and genuinely few students finish it. OPTION-SET TELL, same shape as GEOH2-15: {64.4, 4.4, 16.4, 48.0} with 64.4 - 48.0 = 16.4 exactly. The sector and the triangle are both sitting in the option set, so the key is recoverable by subtracting two options - skipping the arcsin, which is the entire difficulty. Two of four options should be re-chosen; this is the more serious of the two instances because the leak bypasses a harder step.

GEOH2-20.note: No figure. 'Inner diameter' and the liter conversion in the stem leave nothing ambiguous. Medium, closer to easy: one cylinder volume with two conversion traps. 15.7 (diameter used as radius) is the classic and is worth the slot; 3.1 (lateral surface area read as a volume) is a real conceptual error; 1.6 (r instead of r^2) is thinner but is a recognisable slip. Note the key 3.9 and the distractor 3.1 are close enough that a student who rounds sloppily mid-calculation could land between them - not an exclusivity problem, since the stem asks for the nearest tenth and the two values are 0.8 apart.

GEOH2-21.note: No figure; lamp, person, shadow tip on level ground is a configuration students have seen, and the stem is unambiguous. I checked internal consistency: H=4.68 from position one, and position two gives d=2.4, which is indeed closer than 4 m, so 'walks toward the lamp' is satisfied - the item is not self-contradictory. Medium: two similar-triangle setups chained through H, with the only subtlety being that the far leg is d+shadow, not d. 4.7 (H itself) and 3.9 (distance to the new shadow tip) are both one-step-short endpoints; 0.9 is a named misuse of the 4 m.

GEOH2-22.note: No figure; both circles are given algebraically. Medium: distance between centres (an 6-8-10 that falls out instantly) minus both radii. The only insight is that the minimum lies along the centre line, and that is standard. 10 (centres only), 4 (one radius removed), 18 (the maximum instead of the minimum) are three clean paths. The option set does contain 10 and 2, i.e. the centre distance and the answer, but the stem already gives both radii, so nothing is reconstructed that the stem withheld.

GEOH2-23.note: No figure. Medium: two sine evaluations and a subtraction. The 1.5 m hand height is a deliberate red herring that cancels in the difference - a nice touch, but it adds a step rather than a difficulty. 68.6 (the later height instead of the change) is a strong trap and 22.3 (cosine for sine, i.e. horizontal change) is a real confusion; 16.0, the angle difference 50-34 relabelled as meters, corresponds to no procedure a student who has got this far would execute, and it is the one weak option in the set. Dropped to plausible on that.

GEOH2-24.note: FIGURE QUESTION, and the most load-bearing case in the batch: there is no figure, and the stem describes the plane purely in words ('the three vertices adjacent to one particular vertex'). I could read it unambiguously - that phrase determines the corner tetrahedron exactly - but it demands 3D visualisation with no support, and a figure would change the measured difficulty materially. Hard either way: the student must see that each pair of those vertices is joined by a FACE DIAGONAL, hence an equilateral triangle of side 6sqrt2, and then apply the equilateral-area formula. 15.6 (edge used as the side, i.e. half the key) is the sharpest distractor; 36.0 (a face) and 18.0 (half a face) catch students who never leave two dimensions. Note 31.2 = 2 x 15.6, so the option set contains a doubling relation, but unlike items 15 and 19 it does not tell you which of the pair is the key.
